title: Freehold covenants
subtitle: The gap the common law left, and how practice papered over it
objectives: Explain why the burden of a freehold covenant cannot run with the land at common law, and how the benefit can
State the requirements for the burden of a restrictive covenant to bind successors in equity under Tulk v Moxhay, and for the benefit to pass under s 78 LPA 1925 and Federated Homes
Identify and apply the practical workarounds used where a positive covenant needs to bind a successor, and the grounds for discharge or modification under s 84 LPA 1925

leadingAuthorities.role: Equity enforces the burden of a restrictive covenant against a successor with notice, to protect land the covenantee retains
Confirms the burden of a positive covenant cannot run with freehold land, at law or in equity

leadingAuthorities.citation: Federated Homes v Mill Lodge [1980] 1 WLR 594
leadingAuthorities.role: Holds that s 78 LPA 1925 annexes the benefit of a covenant automatically to each part of the retained land
A successor who takes the benefit of a right must also accept the correlative burden — the mutual benefit and burden principle

leadingAuthorities.citation: Alexander Devine Children's Cancer Trust v Housing Solutions [2020] UKSC 45
leadingAuthorities.role: Supreme Court confirms the narrow scope of the mutual benefit and burden principle and of discharge under s 84

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can state 'the burden of a positive covenant doesn't run' as a rule. Where the profile shows knowledge ahead of application, this note appears: 'You know the rule — this lesson is about the workarounds that make it survive in practice anyway.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on the rule itself before. The test pool below leans on application: expect fact patterns asking whether a specific workaround actually rescues a positive covenant, not just whether the rule exists.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take the historical framing seriously — the workarounds in Parts 3 and 4 only make sense once you understand precisely what gap they're patching.

overview.hook: A developer sells forty houses on a new estate, each buyer promising in the transfer deed to keep their roof in good repair and to contribute to the cost of the shared private road. Thirty years and six changes of ownership later, one owner lets the roof rot and refuses to pay a penny towards the road. The original buyer who made that promise is long gone. Can anyone still enforce it? The common law's answer is a flat no — and this lesson is about everything conveyancers invented to get around that no.

parts.heading: The rule: a promise about freehold land dies with the person who made it
parts.voice: historical — starts from the common law's structural commitment and only then shows its cost
body: Leasehold law solved this problem centuries ago: covenants in a lease can bind successive tenants and landlords, because the relationship of landlord and tenant gives the law a peg to hang continuing obligations on. Freehold land has no such peg. Once a freehold owner sells, the common law's traditional position is that privity of contract — the relationship that made the original promise enforceable — ends with the sale. The buyer's successor was never a party to that promise and, at common law, cannot be bound by it.

This is sometimes shortened to 'the burden of a covenant does not run with freehold land,' and it survived a direct challenge in the House of Lords. In Rhone v Stephens, a covenant to keep a roof (spanning two divided halves of a house) in repair, made by the original owner, was held unenforceable against her successor — even though the successor's half of the roof needed the promise to function. Lord Templeman was blunt: equity can restrain the doing of something (a restrictive, negative obligation), but it has never compelled a successor to spend money performing a positive act they never agreed to.

Notice what survives from this: the benefit of a covenant — the right to enforce it — can run with land far more readily than the burden can. The asymmetry is the whole story of this lesson. The law is comparatively generous about who can sue; it is famously stingy about who can be sued, at least for a positive promise.

components.definition: The principle that only the original parties to a contract (here, the original covenantor and covenantee) can sue or be sued on it — the reason a successor in title is not automatically bound by a predecessor's promise.

components.factsShort: A house was divided; the seller covenanted to keep the roof, which spanned both halves, in repair for the benefit of the part she was selling off. Her successor in title to the retained half let the roof fall into disrepair.
components.ratioShort: The burden of a positive covenant cannot run with freehold land, either at common law or in equity — equity restrains, it does not compel expenditure.

expanded.facts: A house known as Walcot House was divided into a main house and a smaller cottage. The seller of the cottage covenanted to keep the roof over both parts in repair. Decades later, the seller's successor in title to the main house — bound by no direct contract with the cottage owner — allowed the roof to deteriorate, causing damage to the cottage below.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lord Templeman held that equity, following Tulk v Moxhay, only ever restrained the doing of an act inconsistent with a covenant — it never compelled a successor to spend money carrying out repairs they had not personally promised. To extend equitable enforcement to positive covenants would be to rewrite the doctrine, not apply it.
expanded.significance: This closed off any argument that Tulk v Moxhay's equitable jurisdiction had quietly grown wide enough to catch positive covenants. It is the leading modern authority that the burden of a positive freehold covenant simply does not run, at law or in equity, and that any solution has to come from outside the covenant itself.

interaction.prompt: State, in one sentence, why the burden of a covenant does not automatically bind a freehold successor in title at common law.
acceptableAnswers: privity of contract ends with the original parties
no privity of contract or estate between successor and covenantee
successor was not a party to the original promise
interaction.modelAnswer: Because privity of contract exists only between the original covenantor and covenantee, and a successor in title — never having made the promise themselves — is not automatically bound by it.

parts.heading: The benefit: who inherits the right to enforce
parts.voice: doctrinal — traces how a narrow common law rule was widened by a single statutory word
body: If the burden struggles to run, the benefit runs comparatively easily — at both law and equity — provided three conditions are met: the covenant must touch and concern the land (benefiting the land itself, not merely the original covenantee personally), the original covenantee must have held a legal estate in the benefited land, and the parties must have intended the benefit to run with that land.

That third condition — intention — used to require careful drafting: a covenant expressly stated to benefit 'the covenantee and their successors in title.' Federated Homes v Mill Lodge changed the practical stakes enormously. The Court of Appeal held that s 78 Law of Property Act 1925 — which deems a covenant to be made with the covenantee 'and the persons deriving title under him' — does not merely describe who can sue; it actively annexes the benefit of a qualifying covenant to every part of the retained land automatically, whether or not the conveyance says so in as many words.

The practical effect is that intention to benefit successors is now presumed by statute for most covenants entered into after 1925, unless the deed shows a contrary intention. This is why modern practice spends less energy drafting elaborate benefit clauses than older textbooks might suggest — s 78 usually does that work unprompted, provided the covenant genuinely touches and concerns the retained land.

components.text: A covenant relating to any land of the covenantee shall be deemed to be made with the covenantee and his successors in title and the persons deriving title under him or them, and shall have effect as if such successors and other persons were expressed.
elements: A covenant relating to (touching and concerning) land of the covenantee
Deemed made with successors in title and those deriving title under them
Effective as if those successors were expressly named

components.caseName: Federated Homes Ltd v Mill Lodge Properties Ltd
components.factsShort: A developer covenanted not to build more than a fixed number of houses on retained land, for the benefit of an estate being sold off in phases. A later owner of part of the estate sought to enforce the covenant, without an express assignment of its benefit.
components.ratioShort: Section 78 LPA 1925 automatically annexes the benefit of a qualifying covenant to each and every part of the covenantee's retained land, without needing an express annexation clause.

expanded.facts: The developer, Mill Lodge Properties, had covenanted with the seller not to build beyond a specified density on land it retained. The benefit of that covenant had not been expressly assigned when part of the benefited estate was later sold on to Federated Homes, who then sought to enforce it directly against Mill Lodge's successor.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Brightman LJ held that s 78 was not a mere word-saving conveyancing shorthand — on its natural wording, it operates to annex the benefit of the covenant to the land itself, and therefore to every part of it, at the moment the covenant is made, without needing the parties to draft an express annexation clause.
expanded.significance: This is the leading authority for statutory annexation. It dramatically reduced the drafting risk around benefit-passing and remains the standard starting point for whether a successor can enforce a covenant they never expressly took an assignment of.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that, after Federated Homes, an express annexation clause is still legally necessary for the benefit of a qualifying post-1925 covenant to pass to successors?
sliderLabels: Definitely not necessary — s 78 does it automatically
interaction.explanation: Federated Homes held that s 78 annexes the benefit automatically to qualifying covenants, without an express clause — though careful drafting can still exclude s 78 by showing a contrary intention.

parts.heading: Tulk v Moxhay: equity's one-doctrine fix for the burden
parts.voice: problem-and-solution — frames the gap first, then shows exactly how equity closed part of it
body: If the common law flatly refuses to bind a successor to a promise they never made, how did Leicester Square end up with a permanent, enforceable promise never to build on it — a promise that has outlived everyone who signed it by over a century? The answer is equity, acting nearly twenty years before the burden-of-covenant problem even had a name.

In Tulk v Moxhay, the seller of a garden square covenanted, as a condition of sale, to keep it as an open pleasure ground. Successive buyers took the land with notice of that promise, and one of them proposed to build on it. The Court of Chancery restrained him — not because the common law recognised the covenant as running with the land, but because it would be unconscionable for a buyer who took land cheaper precisely because of the restriction, with knowledge of it, to then ignore it.

That equitable jurisdiction survived and hardened into a doctrine with four conditions: the covenant must be negative in substance (restraining an act, not compelling expenditure — this is exactly the line Rhone v Stephens later drew hard), it must accommodate (touch and concern) land retained by the covenantee, the original parties must have intended the burden to run, and the successor must take with notice of the covenant — a condition now effectively satisfied by registration, since an unregistered restrictive covenant affecting registered land will not bind a purchaser for value.

Notice the shape of the fix and its limit in the same sentence: equity will stop a successor from doing something the land was never supposed to do — but it will never make them pay for or perform something positive. That limit is precisely why the next part of this lesson exists.

components.label: The four Tulk v Moxhay conditions
points: The covenant is negative (restrictive) in substance — restrains an act, requires no expenditure to comply
The covenant accommodates (touches and concerns) land retained by the covenantee
The original parties intended the burden to bind successors in title
The successor took the servient land with notice of the covenant (satisfied today by registration of the restriction)

interaction.prompt: A seller of a plot covenants, as a condition of sale, never to use the retained neighbouring plot for anything other than residential purposes, in order to protect the value of the land being sold. The seller's successor in title to the retained plot, who took with notice of the covenant (it is duly registered), now wants to open a shop there. Analyse whether the covenant's burden binds the successor.
factsToOrder: The covenant restrains a use (no non-residential use) rather than requiring expenditure
The covenant was intended to protect the value of the land sold — it accommodates that land
The original parties intended the burden to bind successors
The successor took the retained plot with notice via registration

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the burden of the restrictive covenant against non-residential use binds the successor in title to the retained plot.
modelAnswer.rule: Under Tulk v Moxhay, the burden of a covenant binds a successor in equity where the covenant is negative in substance, accommodates land retained by the covenantee, the original parties intended the burden to run, and the successor took with notice.
modelAnswer.application: The covenant restrains a use rather than compelling any expenditure, so it is negative in substance. It was made to protect the value of the land sold, so it accommodates that land. Registration of the restriction satisfies both the intention-to-bind and notice requirements on these facts.
modelAnswer.conclusion: All four Tulk v Moxhay conditions are satisfied; the burden binds the successor, who cannot lawfully open a shop on the retained plot.

parts.heading: Papering over the gap: what happens when the covenant is positive
parts.voice: practitioner's-toolkit — surveys each workaround honestly, including where it fails
body: Tulk v Moxhay never rescues a positive covenant — a promise to build a fence, repair a roof, or pay towards a shared road. Since Rhone v Stephens confirmed that gap is permanent, conveyancers have relied on a small set of workarounds, none of them as clean as a rule that simply bound the land.

The oldest and weakest is the chain of indemnity covenant: each seller, on selling on, takes a fresh covenant from their buyer to observe the original positive covenant and to indemnify the seller if they don't. In theory this passes the obligation down an unbroken chain of personal contracts. In practice the chain is only as strong as its weakest link — miss one indemnity covenant on one sale in the chain, or find that seller has since become untraceable or insolvent, and the whole mechanism collapses for everyone further down.

The more durable workaround is the mutual benefit and burden principle from Halsall v Brizell: a successor who wants to take the benefit of a right (for instance, using a shared private road or drainage system) must accept the burden that comes attached to it (contributing to its upkeep) — they cannot cherry-pick the advantage and refuse the cost. This isn't really an exception to the no-burden rule at all; it's a form of conditional benefit, closer to contract than to covenant.

The Supreme Court kept that principle on a tight leash in Alexander Devine Children's Cancer Trust v Housing Solutions. It confirmed that mutual benefit and burden only works where there is a genuine, relevant correlation between the specific benefit taken and the specific burden imposed — a successor cannot be saddled with an unrelated positive obligation simply because they benefit from something else nearby. The case also addressed the s 84 jurisdiction to discharge or modify covenants, holding that a landowner cannot rely on their own breach (building affordable housing in deliberate disregard of a known restrictive covenant) to argue the covenant should now be modified because the building already exists — a point the next part of this lesson develops.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often say Halsall v Brizell means any successor who benefits at all from a development can be made to pay towards any of its positive obligations.
components.whyItsWrong: Alexander Devine confirms the principle is narrow: the burden must be conditional on, and correlated with, the specific benefit actually taken up. A successor who never uses the shared road cannot be forced to contribute to it merely because they live nearby and benefit from the estate generally.

interaction.prompt: Which of these is the best statement of the mutual benefit and burden principle after Alexander Devine?
options: Any owner who benefits in any way from an estate's amenities can be required to perform any positive covenant attached to that estate
A successor who chooses to take up a specific benefit (such as using a shared facility) can be required to accept the specific, correlated burden attached to that benefit
The principle was abolished by Alexander Devine and replaced entirely by s 84 modification
interaction.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answer treats the principle as a general 'benefit from the estate, pay for the estate' rule. Alexander Devine confirms it is much narrower — the benefit taken and the burden imposed must be specifically and relevantly correlated, not merely both connected to the same development.

parts.heading: Ending a covenant: discharge and modification under s 84
parts.voice: closing — treats this as the release valve for a system built on permanence
body: A restrictive covenant that binds in equity binds indefinitely, by default — there's no automatic expiry. That permanence is workable for a genuinely timeless restriction (keep this as parkland), but can strand land under an obligation that made sense in 1960 and makes none in 2026, with the original parties long dead and untraceable.

Section 84 Law of Property Act 1925 gives the Upper Tribunal (Lands Chamber) jurisdiction to discharge or modify a restrictive covenant on specified grounds: that changes in the character of the property or neighbourhood have made the covenant obsolete; that the covenant impedes some reasonable use of the land and either secures no practical benefit of substantial value to those entitled to enforce it, or is contrary to the public interest; that those entitled to the benefit have agreed, expressly or by implication; or that discharge or modification will not injure the persons entitled to the benefit.

Alexander Devine is the sharpest recent illustration of the limits of this jurisdiction. A developer built housing in deliberate breach of a known restrictive covenant protecting a neighbouring children's hospice, then applied under s 84 to have the covenant modified on the basis that the housing already existed and demolishing it would be wasteful. The Supreme Court refused: a deliberate, cynical breach cannot be used to manufacture the very facts (a completed building whose removal seems disproportionate) that are then relied on to justify modification. The jurisdiction exists to relieve genuinely outdated restrictions, not to reward parties who build first and ask permission later.

The section applies only to restrictive covenants — a further reminder that positive covenants sit almost entirely outside this statutory scheme too, and depend on whichever of the Part 4 workarounds was built into the original transaction, if any was.

components.text: The Upper Tribunal shall ... have power ... to discharge or modify any [restrictive] covenant ... on being satisfied— (a) that ... the covenant ought to be deemed obsolete; or (aa) that ... the continued existence [of the covenant] would impede some reasonable user of the land ... and that the covenant, in impeding that user, either does not secure to persons entitled to the benefit of it any practical benefits of substantial value ... or is contrary to the public interest ...; or (b) that the persons ... entitled to the benefit of the covenant have agreed ...; or (c) that the proposed discharge or modification will not injure the persons entitled to the benefit of the covenant.
elements: Ground (aa): impedes reasonable use, and no substantial practical benefit or contrary to public interest
Ground (c): no injury to those entitled to the benefit

interaction.prompt: A developer builds a block of flats in known, deliberate breach of a restrictive covenant protecting a neighbour's light and outlook, then applies under s 84 to modify the covenant, arguing that demolishing the completed flats now would be wasteful and disproportionate. Following Alexander Devine, how should this application be treated?
options: The completed building is itself strong evidence favouring modification, since demolition would now be wasteful
The deliberate breach cannot be used to manufacture the facts relied on to justify modification — the tribunal should not reward building first and asking later
Section 84 has no application at all once any building has commenced, regardless of the circumstances
interaction.explanation: Alexander Devine held that a party cannot deliberately breach a covenant, complete the prohibited building, and then point to the fait accompli as a reason to modify the covenant — that would let cynical breach manufacture its own justification.

testPool.prompt: State the general common law rule about whether the burden of a freehold covenant runs with the land.
acceptableAnswers: the burden of a covenant does not run with freehold land at common law
burden does not bind successors at law
testPool.modelAnswer: The burden of a freehold covenant does not run with the land at common law; a successor in title is not automatically bound by a predecessor's promise, because they were not a party to it.

testPool.prompt: Can the burden of a positive covenant (e.g. to repair a roof) run with freehold land in equity, following Rhone v Stephens?
options: No — equity restrains acts, it does not compel expenditure
Yes — equity treats positive and restrictive covenants identically

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the four Tulk v Moxhay conditions for the burden of a covenant to bind in equity?
options: The covenant is negative (restrictive) in substance
The covenant accommodates land retained by the covenantee
The covenant has been registered for at least twenty years
The successor took with notice of the covenant
testPool.trapExplanation: There is no twenty-year requirement anywhere in Tulk v Moxhay — that figure belongs to prescription in the law of easements, not to the equitable enforcement of restrictive covenants, which turns on notice, not time.

testPool.prompt: What did Federated Homes v Mill Lodge hold that s 78 LPA 1925 actually does?
options: It merely lists who is entitled to sue, without changing whether the benefit passes automatically
It automatically annexes the benefit of a qualifying covenant to every part of the covenantee's retained land, without needing an express clause
It abolishes the touch-and-concern requirement for the benefit of a covenant to pass
testPool.explanation: Federated Homes read s 78 as substantively annexing the benefit at the moment the covenant is made, not merely describing who could later be assigned it.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that states the ratio on the burden of a positive covenant.
testPool.passage: The claimant argued that equity's willingness to enforce restrictive covenants against successors should extend, by analogy, to a positive covenant to repair. The House of Lords disagreed. Equity, following Tulk v Moxhay, has only ever restrained the doing of an act inconsistent with a covenant; it has never compelled a successor to expend money in carrying out repairs or other positive works they did not themselves promise to perform. The claim against the successor accordingly failed.
testPool.ratioSentence: Equity, following Tulk v Moxhay, has only ever restrained the doing of an act inconsistent with a covenant; it has never compelled a successor to expend money in carrying out repairs or other positive works they did not themselves promise to perform.

testPool.prompt: Order the steps a court follows when asked whether the burden of a restrictive covenant binds a successor under Tulk v Moxhay.
items: Check the covenant is negative in substance, not positive
Check the covenant accommodates land retained by the covenantee
Check the original parties intended the burden to bind successors
Check the successor took the land with notice of the covenant

testPool.prompt: Which covenant is capable of binding a successor's burden directly under Tulk v Moxhay, without needing any workaround?
testPool.scenarioA: A covenant not to build above two storeys on the retained plot, made to protect the covenantee's light and view, registered against the title.
testPool.scenarioB: A covenant to pay an annual sum towards maintaining a shared private road serving both plots.
testPool.explanation: A is negative in substance (it restrains building) and fits Tulk v Moxhay directly. B is a positive obligation to pay money, which Rhone v Stephens confirms cannot bind a successor's burden under Tulk v Moxhay — it needs a workaround such as mutual benefit and burden.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that is essential to a successful mutual benefit and burden argument under Halsall v Brizell.
testPool.scenarioText: A homeowner on an estate has never used the estate's shared private drainage system, relying instead on their own separate connection, but the estate management company demands they contribute towards the drainage system's upkeep regardless.
tappableSpans: has never used the estate's shared private drainage system
relying instead on their own separate connection
the estate management company demands they contribute
testPool.correctSpan: has never used the estate's shared private drainage system
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right. Mutual benefit and burden only bites where the successor actually takes up the correlated benefit — a homeowner who never uses the shared system cannot be forced to pay for it under this principle.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact about whether the benefit is actually being used. The principle is conditional: no benefit taken, no burden imposed — regardless of what the management company demands.

testPool.prompt: A buyer of a plot on an estate covenants to pay a service charge towards the upkeep of a shared driveway, and each subsequent seller has, without fail, taken a matching indemnity covenant from their buyer on every sale since. The current owner refuses to pay. What is the main practical weakness in enforcing the original covenant against them via this mechanism?
options: The chain of indemnity covenants only works if every link in the chain is intact and each covenantor remains solvent and traceable — one broken or unenforceable link defeats the whole chain
Indemnity covenants are void under the Law of Property Act 1925
Chains of indemnity covenants can only be used for restrictive, not positive, covenants
testPool.explanation: A chain of indemnity covenants is a chain of personal contracts, not a rule that binds the land itself — it is only as strong as its weakest, most recent link.

testPool.prompt: The original covenantee's successor wants to enforce a restrictive covenant made in 1965, protecting the retained land from commercial use. No express assignment of the benefit was ever made on any of the several sales since. Assuming the covenant touches and concerns the land, is the benefit likely to have passed?
options: Yes — s 78 LPA 1925, as interpreted in Federated Homes, annexes the benefit automatically to each part of the retained land
No — without an express assignment on every sale, the benefit is lost permanently
It depends entirely on whether the covenant was registered as a legal easement
testPool.explanation: Federated Homes confirms that s 78 does the annexation work automatically for a qualifying covenant, so an unbroken chain of express assignments is not required.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that s 84 LPA 1925 can be used to discharge or modify a positive covenant, such as an obligation to pay a service charge?
testPool.explanation: Section 84 is confined to restrictive covenants. Positive covenants sit outside its discharge and modification scheme entirely, which is part of why the workarounds in Part 4 matter so much in practice.

testPool.prompt: A developer, fully aware of a registered restrictive covenant limiting a plot to a single dwelling, deliberately builds three houses on it, calculating that a s 84 application afterwards will be cheaper than compliance. The developer now applies under s 84(1)(aa), arguing the covenant impedes reasonable use of the land and that demolishing two of the three houses would be a disproportionate practical consequence. Analyse the application's prospects.
factsToOrder: The developer knew of the covenant before building
The breach was deliberate, not accidental or the result of a genuine mistake
The developer now points to the completed buildings as a reason to modify the covenant
Ground (aa) requires no substantial practical benefit to those entitled to enforce, or that enforcement is contrary to the public interest

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the Upper Tribunal should discharge or modify the covenant under s 84(1)(aa) given the developer's deliberate breach.
modelAnswer.rule: Section 84(1)(aa) permits modification where a restrictive covenant impedes reasonable use and secures no substantial practical benefit, or is contrary to the public interest; Alexander Devine confirms a party cannot rely on their own deliberate breach to manufacture the facts (a completed building whose removal seems disproportionate) used to justify modification.
modelAnswer.application: The developer knew of the covenant and built in deliberate disregard of it, then seeks to use the existence of the completed houses — the direct product of that breach — as the practical argument for modification. This is precisely the cynical-breach scenario Alexander Devine rejected.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The application is very unlikely to succeed; the tribunal should not allow a deliberate breach to generate the disproportionality argument later relied on to excuse it.

testPool.prompt: Which body has jurisdiction under s 84 LPA 1925 to discharge or modify a restrictive covenant?
options: The Upper Tribunal (Lands Chamber)
The Land Registry, on a simple administrative application

testPool.prompt: Which scenario better fits an s 84(1)(a) 'obsolescence' argument, rather than mutual benefit and burden?
testPool.scenarioA: A 1930s covenant restricting a plot to 'agricultural use only' sits in the middle of a now-dense residential town, surrounded entirely by houses built decades ago with no agricultural land left nearby.
testPool.scenarioB: A resident wants to use a shared private tennis court on the estate without paying the agreed annual contribution towards its upkeep.
testPool.explanation: A is a covenant that has been overtaken by a total change in the character of the neighbourhood — the textbook obsolescence ground under s 84(1)(a). B is a benefit-and-burden question about a specific facility, not about the covenant becoming outdated.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best explains why the benefit of a covenant runs with land more readily than the burden does?
options: Because Parliament has simply never legislated on the burden side of covenants at all

Because the law is generally willing to let successors enforce advantages attached to land they hold, but has historically refused to impose fresh personal obligations, especially positive ones, on someone who never agreed to them
Because only the benefit of a covenant can ever be registered against a title
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answers point to registration or legislative silence. The real reason is doctrinal: courts have long been far more comfortable letting land carry an advantage for its owner than compelling an unconsenting successor to perform, or pay for, a positive obligation.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson is applying Tulk v Moxhay to a covenant that is positive in substance. Check the covenant's substance — restrain an act, or compel one — before reaching for any doctrine at all; if it's positive, the analysis moves straight to the Part 4 workarounds, not to Tulk v Moxhay.
